title: vpc-provisioning-idempotency-tf-decision-log
content:
Purpose:
This is a working decision log + runbook fragment for making VPC provisioning and upgrades (private deployments) reliably idempotent with Terraform. Focus: reduce destructive blips during module upgrades, reduce manual state surgery, and make safe rollback patterns prescriptive for oncall and SEs doing customer cutovers.

High-level goals (non-exhaustive):
- Ensure repeated terraform apply runs produce no unexpected resource replacement for the normal upgrade path.
- Provide reactive rollback steps that can be executed with low blast radius when a change causes network disruption.
- Define preflight gates and automated plan analysis to catch destructive diffs before apply.
- Document patterns for multi-account/state, tfstate migration, and provider drift handling.

Context/assumptions:
- Customers use Redwood Private deployed into their VPC, sometimes with an on-prem connector.
- We use multiple Terraform workspaces for customer envs (customer-<id>-staging, -prod). Some customers request a single shared state for network resources; we strongly recommend separate state for tenant-specific routing/peering.
- Provider versions vary (aws, azure, gcp). We must support differences in lifecycle rules (eg aws_vpc vs gcp_network).

Decisions (so far):
1) Module pinning and major-version upgrade policy
   - Pin module major versions in platform repo (eg vpc-module v2.x). Patch/minor updates can be pulled automatically by dependabot + CI acceptance tests.
   - Major-version bumps require a migration PR with a documented incremental plan entry and a canary rollout for 2 low-risk tenants before wider rollout.

2) Apply orchestration and state locking
   - All applies must run under a CI pipeline (not manual local) that enforces state locking and runs plan-analysis hooks.
   - Use remote state with locking (S3+Dynamo for AWS, GCS+CloudLocks for GCP). Avoid local/backups as canonical during maintenance.

3) Preflight checks & plan linting
   - Fail CI/automation if plan contains: resource deletions of core shared VPC (subnets, route tables, main IGW) or replacement of primary route table association.
   - Implement plan-parsing script that looks for >N resource replacements (N configurable, default 3) and flags for manual review.

4) Safe replacement patterns (preferred)
   - For resources where terraform forces replacement (eg change of cidr block), use blue-green style pattern where new resources are created, dependencies switched over, and old ones destroyed once traffic is verified. The module should expose a "migration" boolean parameter to trigger this path.

5) Rollback primitives
   - Prefer revert-by-apply (apply previous module version with same inputs) over state manipulation.
   - When state surgery is unavoidable, provide explicit terraform state mv/rm command sequences in the runbook and require a state backup snapshot commit.

Checklist: Pre-apply (automated)
- terraform validate + fmt
- terraform plan output captured to artifact
- run plan-lint: no unexpected destroy/replace for protected resource list
- smoke test workspace: spin ephemeral VPC in staging account and run connectivity tests (ping/gRPC handshake to a test endpoint, routing table checks)
- confirm provider version compatibility matrix for this customer

Checklist: Manual gating before prod apply
- SE/owner assigns a time window (low-traffic) and notifies customer and SRE rotation
- Snapshot current tfstate and upload to archive bucket (timestamped and signed)
- Ensure route table and LB healthchecks have fallback tolerances enabled (eg connection draining where applicable)
- Verify canary tenants have run the same upgrade without issues for 24h

Rollback runbook (fast path)
1) If the apply produced network degradation that can be fixed by reverting module version: submit CI PR that pins previous module tag with same inputs and run apply. Monitor.
2) If apply introduced partial resource replacements and revert-by-apply is not possible: restore tfstate snapshot to a new workspace and run a plan to detect drift (requires SRE coordination).
3) State surgery (last resort): perform documented terraform state mv/rm with backup. Steps must be run under SRE approval and recorded in incident.

Testing harness ideas (todo items to implement):
- A small terraform test-suite that runs against an isolated test account and simulates: module-major-upgrade, provider-upgrade, CIDR-shrink/expand, peering removal/recreate, and route-table replacement. Test suite should surface the exact operation type (create/replace/destroy) per resource and produce a recommended remediation (eg add lifecycle ignore_changes or migration flag).
- A "dry-run network simulator" that parses plan JSON and runs a lightweight reachability model: if route A->B is to be replaced, simulate transient reachability with current + post-change configs to highlight windows where traffic might drop.

Common failure patterns we've observed (notes):
- Changing a subnet's map_public_ip_on_launch causes instances to lose external connectivity (we now recommend creating new subnets and migrating ENIs).
- Moving from one route table association to another caused ephemeral control-plane loss for on-prem connectors because BGP sessions reset. Workaround: schedule BGP session re-establishment and use longer hold-timers where possible.
- Terraform provider minor updates changing default lifecycle behavior (eg resource recreation on name change). Pin provider minor if test-suite fails.

Operational conventions (team norms):
- All migration PRs must include a one-paragraph risk summary and rollback anchor commands at top of PR description.
- For customer onboarding, the SE runbook must include a stubbed terraform workspace with exact backend config and a small script to produce a state snapshot and a restore script (customer-specific variables must be redacted).

Outstanding decisions / unresolved questions:
- Should we standardize on a single global policy for plan-block thresholds (replacements >3) or make per-customer? Tradeoff: safety vs agility. (Priya to prototype a per-customer YAML override.)
- How do we safely handle CIDR changes for customers who require overlapping address space reductions? Can we offer an automated ENI migration helper? (Diego investigating feasibility.)
- Who owns the canonical archive of tfstate snapshots? Ops currently, but needs formal SLA and retention policy.

Action items (next steps):
- (Ava) Draft CI plan-lint script and add to infra repo as proof-of-concept. Target: 2026-03-15.
- (Priya) Prototype terraform test-suite against test account and report resource replacement counts. Target: 2026-04-01.
- (Samir) Draft SRE approval flow for state surgery and add to oncall playbook. Target: 2026-03-22.
- (Jules) Add docs for provider pinning and a sample rollback PR template. Target: 2026-03-30.

Notes-to-self / scratch:
- keep the migration flag in modules minimal; too many toggles lead to combinatorial testing hell.
- consider exposing a read-only "migration-plan" output from modules that lists resources that will be recreated if flag toggled. Useful for SEs when talking to customers.

References and snippets (examples that should be added to infra repo):
- sample plan-lint snippet: parse plan JSON for "replace": true entries and match against protected_resources list
- sample state backup: aws s3 cp statebucket/customer-id/terraform.tfstate state-backups/customer-id/tfstate-20260228.json --sse aws:kms

If you are reviewing this doc: add comments inline, mark items you want to own, and link related PRs. This is intentionally pragmatic and a bit messy; goal is to capture tacit knowledge before it becomes tribal.

Last note: this is intentionally focused on making the failure modes predictable. We will follow up with a short customer-facing checklist for onboarding (what we ask customers to do in their VPC ahead of Redwood Private deployment).
